headline: Approved public notice to lay out right-of-way over 1720 Spear Street and a Step 3 downtown grant application.
summary: Residents raised water pressure and flow complaints after the Brewer Parkway water main project, and the Council asked staff to look into them. The Council discussed a possible CHIP application for the O'Brien Farm Project and took no vote. The Council approved the consent agenda and the public notice for 1720 Spear Street.
decisions: Approved the consent agenda, including $11,190 for garage bay doors at DPW, unanimously.
Approved the public notice to institute proceedings over 1720 Spear Street and set a public hearing, 4-0.
Approved Resolution 2026-15 authorizing a Step 3 downtown application, unanimously.
Continued to a future agenda the proposed hiring of outside counsel for building and thermal work.
Moved the Legislative Advocacy Agenda to the next meeting.

decision_evidence.quote: Mr. Chalnick moved to approve the Consent Agenda as presented. Ms. Fitzgerald seconded. Motion passed unanimously.

Mr. Smith moved to approve the public notice to institute proceedings regarding the laying out of right-of-way depicted on Official Map over 1720 Spear Street, and to set a public hearing for 6 November 2026 at Noon. Dr. Zigmund seconded. The motion passed 4-0.

Mr. Chalnick moved to approve Resolution 2026-15 and authorize the City Manager to submit an application to Vermont Department of Housing and Community Development for a City Center downtown area. Mr. Smith seconded. The motion passed unanimously.
Mr. Barritt said as this is totally unexpected, he asked to put it on a future agenda. Members agreed.
Mr. Smith asked to move this item to the next meeting agenda.

plain_text:
PAGE 1 
DRAFT MINUTES 
 CITY COUNCIL 
      19 OCTOBER 2026 
 
The South Burlington City Council held a regular meeting on Monday, 19 October  
2026, at 6:30 p.m., in the Auditorium, 180 Market Street, and by Zoom. 
 
MEMBERS PRESENT: T. Barritt, Chair; E. Fitzgerald, L. Smith, A. Chalnick, Dr. B. 
Zigmund 
 
ALSO PRESENT: J. Baker, City Manager; N. Storellicastro, Deputy City Manager; P. 
Conner, Director of Planning & Zoning; C. McNeil, City Attorney; I. Blanchard, 
Community Development Director; E. Towle, Public Works Director; B. McCreary, 
Water Resources; B. Miguez, Climate Action Manager; S. Crowley, T. Rizzo, A. 
Treston, S. Smith-Conroy, S. Julius, B. Sigrino, A. Caldwell, M. Jacobson, J. 
McCown, R. Moulton, P. Sallers, E. Langfeldt, A. Gill, J. McClory  
 
1. Pledge of Allegiance: 
 
The Pledge of Allegiance was recited. 
 
2. Instructions on exiting building in case of emergency and review of 
technology options: 
 
Mr. Storellicastro provided instructions on emergency exit from the building and 
reviewed technology options. 
  
3. Additions, deletions or changes in the order of Agenda items: 
 
No changes were made to the Agenda. 
 
4. Comments and questions from the public not related to the agenda:
CITY COUNCIL 19 October 2026 PAGE 2 
Mr. Crowley of the Energy Committee drew attention to a recent article in the 
Journal of Bioscience regarding the destabilization of the earth’s surface which 
affirms the work the City of South Burlington is doing and encourages doing 
more. Mr. Chalnick said he looks forward to the Energy Committee bringing 
proposals. 
 
Ms. Treston, an East Terrace resident, said there is now a 25 mph sign on their 
street, which is good; however, the parking situation has gotten worse.  Residents 
would like to hear a plan from the Council at its 2 November meeting. 
 
5. Councilors Announcements and Reports on Committee Assignments                                                        
and City Manager’s Report: 
 
Council members reported on recent meetings and events they had attended. 
 
Mr. Storellicastro: Noted that Ms. Baker would be attending this meeting 
remotely. 
 
  As of today, there are 90 responses to the Budget Survey.  The 
Survey will be up for 10 more days. 
 
6. Consent Agenda: 
a. Consider and Sign Disbursements 
b. Approve the allocation of $11,190 of ARPA Inspired Fund Balance 
for the repair of garage bay doors at DPW 
c. Award Williston Road Water Valve Construction Contract 
 
Mr. Chalnick moved to approve the Consent Agenda as presented.  Ms. Fitzgerald 
seconded.  Motion passed unanimously. 
 
7. Interview candidates to serve on the Development Review Board: 
 
The Council interviewed Jennifer McClory for the open position on the 
Development Review Board. 
 
8. Receive a Presentation from Brewer Parkway residents on the recent 
water main project: 
 
Mr. Storellicastro reviewed the history of the project, noting that its main focus 
was to restore the condition of hydrants.  Since the project was done, residents
CITY COUNCIL 19 October 2026 PAGE 3 
have noted issues with water pressure and flow.  Mr. Storellicastro said the flow 
issue is the result of the size of the pipe, and this will continue until a second pipe 
is installed. 
 
Other issues that have been raised by residents include site restoration, the 
planting of a tree, a property that has been using 1000 gallons of water per day 
(80 is the norm), and frustration with the project contractor.   
 
Mr. Storellicastro said long term solutions include fixing the flow which would 
require replacing the existing line ($820,000) or connecting to Spear Street 
($1,200,000) or both ($2,000,000). 
 
Mr. Barritt asked if there could be corrosion restricting the flow.  Mr. McCreary 
said that is what they saw in a situation on Shelburne Road.  He noted that this 
project did not replace the entire length of the water main. 
 
Dr. Zigmund asked if there is potential mitigation at the top of the hill with pumps 
as was done in her neighborhood.  Mr. McCreary said the City does not own or 
maintain those pumps, but he would check to see if that could be a help.  He 
stressed it would be at the homeowners’ expense.  Mr. Smith there can also be 
pumps in homes and asked if that is allows.  Mr. McCreary said that is regulated 
by the State.  He said he would look to see is there are options. 
 
Ms. Fitzgerald asked if there are routine inspections and/or other neighborhoods 
with similar issues.  Mr. MrCreary said they inspect regularly.  He could not recall 
any other neighborhoods with neighborhood-wide issues. 
 
With regard to the home using 1000 gpd, Mr. McCreary said that has now 
stopped.   
 
Comments from residents were then solicited and received as follows: 
 
Ms. Smith-Conroy: Wanted to see the project completed correctly, back to the 
“original condition or better.”  That is not the case now.  Water pressure should 
be what it was before the digging began.  There are homes where toilets now 
can’t be flushed, and residents can do laundry.  Work also needs to be done on 
lawns where there are now sinking spots.  The contractor never rolled uneven 
surfaces, just threw some seed and a lot of hay.  Mr. Poulin said they would be 
back in October, but they have not been.  It is not true that all work was done in
CITY COUNCIL 19 October 2026 PAGE 4 
the City right-of-way.  Some work was done half-way up her driveway.  They were 
unsafe for 5 years, and now it’s worse than before. 
 
Ms. Julius: A wildflower garden that had been transplanted from her late 
mother’s home was destroyed and a memorial bench was moved onto her 
neighbor’s law with no notification.  Poulin vehicles parked in her driveway.  Mr. 
Poulin said he would seed the bank with wildflowers.  He never did.  The 
neighborhood is not like it was before the project.  With a project that big, the City 
should have made sure there was better communication. 
 
Mr. Sigrino: The street was known for its maple trees.  Now there are only a few 
remaining.  Poulin dug a 20 foot hole in his yard so that for 7 months he had to 
drive over the median to get out of the house.  They also took away 2-3 inches of 
topsoil.  He feels that there properties were degraded, not improved.  He added 
that several loads of topsoil could help make him feel “whole” again.  They were 
a “hometown” kind of place and would like to be that way again. 
 
Mr. Caldwell: Thanked the City for restoring the hydrants.  He has an 
architectural and planning background.  He would like to see what the pre- and 
post-construction figures regarding water pressure and flow.   
 
Ms. Jacobson:  Lives at the top of Brewer Parkway.  She read an e-mail from the 
water resources company.  PSI is not the only variable in this situation. 
 
Mr. Moulton: Meeting a legal standard minimum is nothing to brag about.  
The 6-inch pipe has to be replaced with an 8-inch pipe.  He noted there is no 
timeline for this. 
 
Mr. McCown: Had no problem with pressure before the project.  They now 
have problems with the toilet, washer, and dishwasher.  He questioned whether 
some particulate matter could have gotten loose during the project.  Things are 
worse than before. 
 
Mr. Barritt said he hears the issue of lack of communication with the contractor.  
Some damage should have been remediated.  The Council will ask staff to look 
into this and to look into the flow issue. 
 
Mr. McCreary said there is a water system Master Plan.  They do flow checks at 
different times of day throughout the system and look at areas with issues.
CITY COUNCIL 19 October 2026 PAGE 5 
Projects need to be prioritized.  Mr. Barritt said that is a strategic plan, not a 
tactical plan.   
 
Mr. Smith said the project seems to have been a perfect storm, and residents 
need an apology.  Communication and effective remediation are vital.   
 
Ms. Baker said she is responsible for operations of the City.  This is a very 
challenging conversation, pitting residents against staff.  She noted they have 
learned lessons from this project and will take what they have learned tonight and 
come back with more information.  Ms. Baker apologized to the community.  Mr. 
Storellicastro said he felt the City can follow up with the contractor. 
 
Ms. Smith-Conroy said the contractor is very young.  They made many mistakes 
and broke more pipes than they installed.  She hoped the Council could provide a 
date when the remaining issues will be resolved.  She also noted there should not 
have been 5 years with no functioning hydrants. 
 
9. Receive an Update on the Building and Thermal Implementation Plan 
and consider what actions to take parallel: 
 
Ms. Miguez noted that the City applied for and received a Municipal Planning 
Grant which is paying for much of the consultant’s time.  This company has 
worked in Vermont previously, particularly looking at electrification.  They have 
completed the first few phases of the project and have begun the first public 
feedback of the plan.  They will be addressing sequencing, affordability, staffing, 
etc.  Staff’s recommendation is to let the process go through.  There should be a 
draft report in January with completion of the project anticipated in March.  The 
City is also working with two people at VEI, a California consulting firm, who will 
be more involved with implementation. 
 
Mr. Chalnick felt there are things the City should be doing now as this is “life 
support” for the planet.  He then enumerated things he felt the City should do 
now: 
 
a. Understand the City’s authority to do the things it needs to do 
b. Learn how to acquire any authority the City does not now have 
c. Investigate any City Charter changes needed to regulate building 
stock 
d. Acquire more data: how are the City’s ordinances working?  What 
portion of homes are electric?  Can ordinances be improved?
CITY COUNCIL 19 October 2026 PAGE 6 
 
Mr. Chalnick then requested that the Council instruct staff to investigate the City’s 
authority to do things, and to get the needed data. 
 
Mr. Smith agreed with Mr. Chalnick regarding timing and urgency.  He said he 
hears people say “we’re too small to make a difference,” but this is an emergency 
and needs to be pushed.  He also acknowledged the capacity of staff and the need 
to consider affordability for all.  
 
Ms. Fitzgerald said she would continue to look for data, and it would help to build 
consensus with the community.  She stressed the need to prioritize investments 
and act with deliberation not panic. 
 
Mr. Chalnick said they need to know what codes they can adopt.  Mr. McNeil said 
this is work that can be done if it is a Council priority.  Mr. Chalnick asked if it 
would push aside other priorities.  Mr. McNeil said it would keep him from 
working on something else.  Ms. Baker reminded the Council that there is no 
Deputy City Attorney at the moment.  She suggested hiring outside counsel.  
There is a budget for that.  Mr. Chalnick said to do it.  Mr. Smith wanted to see an 
RFP.  Mr. Barritt said as this is totally unexpected, he asked to put it on a future 
agenda.  Members agreed. 
 
Mr. Sellers of Run on Climate said they are ready to help the City implement its 
plan.  They have done work on policies in the country including energy audits at 
time of sale or for rental properties.   
 
Ms. Rizzo, a UVM student also with Run on Climate said she supports the work the 
City is doing.  She said a policy to consider is “energy use disclosure,” knowing 
how much it will cost to heat a home when a property is bought or leased. 
 
NOTE:  The following items were heard out of order but are recorded here in the 
order in which they appear on the Agenda. 
 
10. Possible Action to approve public notice to institute proceedings re: 
laying out of right-of-way depicted on Official Map over 1720 Spear 
Street: 
 
Mr. Chalnick recused himself due to a potential conflict of interest.
CITY COUNCIL 19 October 2026 PAGE 7 
Mr. Storellicastro reviewed the history and noted the City has been engaging with 
the property owner.  The intent of this item is to warn a hearing to institute 
proceedings which will stop the clock.   
 
Mr. McNeil said notice would go to The Other Paper.  The proceedings would start 
on 6 November at a special Noon City Council meeting.  The Council will then 
inspect the property and hear from interested parties.  Discussions with the 
property owner will continue during this process. 
 
Mr. Smith moved to approve the public notice to institute proceedings regarding 
the laying out of right-of-way depicted on Official Map over 1720 Spear Street, 
and to set a public hearing for 6 November 2026 at Noon.  Dr. Zigmund seconded.  
The motion passed 4-0. 
 
Mr. Chalnick rejoined the Council. 
 
11.  Approve the Step 3 Downtown application submittal: 
 
Mr. Conner said this will authorize the City Manager to submit the Step 3 
downtown application which is ready to go.  He was confident the application will 
be granted. 
 
Mr. Chalnick moved to approve Resolution 2026-15 and authorize the City 
Manager to submit an application to Vermont Department of Housing and 
Community Development for a City Center downtown area.  Mr. Smith seconded.  
The motion passed unanimously. 
 
12. Discuss the Old Farm Road Development Agreement and a potential 
CHIP application: 
 
Mr. Storellicastro said the purpose of this item is to refamiliarize the Council with 
the existing Development Agreement, to introduce the Council to the CHIP 
process, and to hear from O’Brien regarding a potential CHIP process.   
 
In August of 2025, the Council approved an agreement to relocate Old Farm Road 
for traffic flow and safety benefits.  It also unlocks potential for additional units 
and commercial development.  The agreement conveys a strip of land to the 
O’Briens, relocates and reconstructs the road, conveys the new road to the City, 
and gives the rest of Old Farm Road to the O’Briens.  A map of the area was 
shown indicating the current and future road.
CITY COUNCIL 19 October 2026 PAGE 8 
 
Mr. Storellicastro then explained that CHIP (Community Housing & Infrastructure 
Program) has become law.  It encourages housing development and is similar to a 
TIF with new incremental property tax revenue financing infrastructure.  Unlike a 
TIF, CHIP can be used only for a single contiguous site and cannot be used within 
a TIF district.  Mr. Storellicastro then showed the guidelines of the program, 
noting that it is the municipality that must submit the application.  The debt must 
be incurred within 5 years with the increment retainment of up to 20 years. 
 
Mr. Langfeldt and Mr. Gill, representing the O’Briens, noted that they are a 70 year 
old company very connected to the South Burlington community.  Mr. Langfeldt 
reviewed what they own in the City.  He then showed a rendering of the O’Brien 
Farm Project including the potential commercial lots.  He reviewed what has 
already been built and what will go elsewhere on the property.  They are now 
building a 100% fossil fuel free neighborhood which is being very well received by 
the market. 
 
Mr. Langfeldt cited the rising costs of construction with the cost to build a home 
being up 45% since 2021.  There is also a problem with trade labor and with 
interest rates which affect people’s ability to purchase.  Materials have gone up 
6.7% in the past 12 months.  All of this impacts their ability to deliver on the 
infrastructure requirements for the project. 
 
The CHIP program which they are requesting would cover the re-orientation of 
Old Farm Road, a public park near the historic barn, the cost of the sidewalk to 
Hinesburg Road, and the rec path from Kennedy Drive to Potash Bridge on Route 
116.  Mr. Langfeldt said it is the perfect tool for their situation.  There would be 43 
homes, and will reduce the cost of those homes.  The increment would be specific 
to those homes, but it would also open up another section of very dynamic 
residential/commercial development.   
 
Dr. Zigmund expressed concern that this diverts education funding, and if the 
homes don’t sell, the taxpayers pay.  In addition, the City has learned that the TIF 
district is not growing at the rate the City had hoped.  Mr. Langfeldt said it is the 
developer who takes on all the debt, not the taxpayers.  If the homes don’t sell, 
O’Brien is on the hook.  He stressed that because of costs, nothing can now be 
built.  This is bad for them and bad for the City as there is no Grand List growth. 
 
Ms. Baker noted that TIF building is growing faster than the City had anticipated.  
She noted that the State will make the education funding whole. Mr. Langfeldt
CITY COUNCIL 19 October 2026 PAGE 9 
added that South Burlington has an education impact fee, and each individual 
home owner is paying $8,000 to $12,000 per unit, so new homes are already 
supporting the local education fund. 
 
Mr. Smith said he is skeptical and will need convincing.  He asked the lot sizes for 
the proposed 43 homes.  Mr. Langfeldt said they are all footprint lots, almost 
single-family condos on 7 or 8 acres.  Mr. Smith asked the size of the units.  Mr. 
Gill said they range from 1500 to 3200 square feet.  They will range in price from a 
high of $600,000 for an 1800 square foot home to $1,300,000 for a 3500 square 
foot home.   
 
Mr. Langfeldt noted they had built some “cottage concept” units (1500 square 
feet) which were lower in price, but they did not sell, so they are being rented. 
 
Mr. Smith said he sees this as shifting the cost of development onto all tax payers, 
and it make it look like the home cost less than it actually does.  He added that 
there are many homes with one or two residents in them.  If there were a place for 
those people to move to, families could have those homes. 
 
Mr. Langfeldt said those are valid points, but they have already delivered the 
affordable units required in the project at a significant loss per unit.  There are 105 
units in this phase, so the 43 is a small number.  Early homes are not turning over 
for even more money.  He stressed that new homes will never be priced for 
everyone.   
 
Mr. Gill said Old Farm Road is an existing city road that they are required to move 
150 feet through ledge.  The development itself did not require the moving of that 
road.  It is that situation which is driving this problem.   
 
Mr. Chalnick said he is also skeptical.  He felt they are taking money from some 
municipal fund and some money from the education fund to build 43 homes 
faster.  He didn’t see this as a good policy.  However, there is also the possibility 
of building the commercial base more quickly.  He would like to see figures on 
that potential. 
 
Ms. Fitzgerald asked if the same electric model would be in the 43 homes.  Mr. 
Langfeldt said it would.  They are doing geothermal wells on site.  Ms. Fitzgerald 
said there are elements of the proposal that address city goals (e.g. connectivity).  
There are also questions, and she wanted to hear more.
CITY COUNCIL 19 October 2026 PAGE 10 
Mr. Barritt said if the City Council is cautiously optimistic about working with the 
O’Briens on a plan, he would support funding for just the moving of the road and 
the sidewalk.  Mr. Langfeldt said they can isolate each element and present a 
variety of options.  Mr. Barritt stressed that the moving of Old Farm Road is an 
impediment to the project.  Mr. Smith questioned whether to move the road at 
citizens’ expense. 
 
Dr. Zigmund said there is a lot of commercial space on Market Street that is still 
vacant and said that is also a risk.  Mr. Barritt said it is the O’Brien’s risk, not the 
city’s. 
 
Mr. Barritt asked if the Council wanted staff to get more granular regarding costs.  
Mr. Smith said he needs to be convinced given everything in the City Plan.  He 
was open to staff doing that.   
 
Mr. Gill stressed that they can build the 43 homes without moving the road.  The 
moving of the road opens up the commercial potential.  With the CHIP, there will 
be a source to repay the loan by opening the commercial possibility.  Mr. 
Langfeldt said the project will allow people to live their lives on one site, being 
able to age and move as needed.  He added that Beta has significant residential 
needs as well as commercial needs.  People will be able to live/work/play on the 
same site.  That is the kind of development the city wants. 
 
Mr. Langfeldt said they would like to parallel creating the application with 
providing information the city needs.  Dr. Zigmund said she didn’t favor starting 
the application now.  Mr. Langfeldt stressed that they can do the modeling, but 
they can’t interact with VEPC; only the city can do that.  He asked to get on an 
upcoming agenda. 
 
13. Legislative Advocacy Agenda: Receive recommended areas for 
Legislative Advocacy and discuss Council priorities: 
 
Mr. Smith asked to move this item to the next meeting agenda.  Ms. Baker asked 
members to send her anything they want for that item. 
 
14. Discuss placing wildlife-friendly bulbs (amber) in the lights at 
Hubbard Park and directing the hours of operation of the lights:
CITY COUNCIL 19 October 2026 PAGE 11 
Dr. Zigmund noted the lights are not yet in, and she wanted to discuss amber 
lights which are better for wildlife.  Ms. Baker said there are related permit 
conditions.  She will get information for the next meeting. 
 
15. Review the significant agenda topics for Council’s 2 November 2026 
City Council Meeting: 
 
a. Receive and possibly approve a Housing Committee 
recommendation that $200,000 be allocated from the Housing 
Trust Fund to the Champlain Housing Trust Dorset Commons 
project 
b. Receive the Chittenden County Planning Commission Annual 
Report 
c. Council requested conversation on housing trends and targets in 
the State, County and City 
d. Town Meeting TV Annual Report and Budget presentation 
e. Legislative Advocacy Agenda.  Discuss Council priorities 
f. Discussion on the Council’s goals for a vacant building and graffiti 
ordinance 
g. Process improvements for high-value (BBWTP, Bridge) and 
reporting 
h. Standardize communication to residents who contact the City 
Council 
 
Mr. Chalnick asked to add discussion of the City’s authority regarding thermal 
regulation. 
 
16. Other Business: 
 
Ms. Fitzgerald noted the Council has not received updates from GMT or the 
Airport in a long time.  Ms. Baker noted that if Ms. Riehle has stepped down from 
the Airport position, the Council will need to appoint someone. 
 
17. Consider entering an Executive Session pursuant to 1 V.S.A. Section 
313(a)(3) for the purpose of discussing appointments to the 
Development Review Board: and 
 
18. Consider entering into Executive Session pursuant to 1 V.S.A. 
Section 313(a)(1)(F) and (2) for the purpose of receiving confidential
CITY COUNCIL 19 October 2026 PAGE 12 
attorney-client communications and discussing the negotiation of 
real estate lease or purchase options, specifically 1720 Spear Street: 
 
Mr. Chalnick moved that the Council make a specific finding that premature 
general public knowledge of:  
 1) The appointment, employment, evaluation of a public officer or 
employee; and 
 2) Confidential attorney-client communications and discussion on the 
negotiating or securing of real estate purchase or lease options 
Would clearly place this public body at a substantial disadvantage.  Mr. Smith 
seconded.  The motion passed unanimously. 
 
Mr. Chalnick then moved that the City Council enter into Executive Session under 
1 V.S.A. Sections 313(a)(3),  (a)(1)(F) and (a)(2) for the purpose of discussing: 
1) Evaluation and Appointment of Candidates for the Development Review 
Board 
2) Confidential attorney-client communications and the negotiating or 
securing of real estate purchase or lease options re: 1720 Spear Street 
 
Inviting Mr. Storellicastro into session with the Council for discussion of the first 
topic; and inviting Mr. Storellicastro, Mr. Conner, Ms. Towle, and Mr. McNeil into 
session with Council for the discussion of the second topic.  Mr. Chalnick will be 
recused from discussion of the second topic.  Mr. Smith seconded.  The motion 
passed unanimously. 
 
The Council entered Executive Session at 10:16 p.m. 
 
Ms. Fitzgerald moved to exit Executive Session.  Mr. Smith seconded.  The motion 
passed unanimously.  The Council exited Executive Session at 11:05 p.m. 
 
As there was no further business to come before the Council Mr. Smith moved to                   
adjourn.  Ms. Fitzgerald seconded.  Motion passed unanimously.  The meeting 
was adjourned at 11:06    p.m.
